L8@P0: 2 L9@P0: University Hospital Heidelberg, Department of L10@P0: Infectious Diseases, Parasitology, Im Neuenheimer Feld L11@P0: 324, 69120 Heidelberg, Germany L12@P0: Summary L13@P0: With 500 000 cases of multidrug-resistant tuberculosis there is an urgent need for attractive targets to L14@P0: enable the discovery of novel antimycobacterials. The L15@P0: biosynthesis of essential cofactors is of particular L16@P0: interest as these pathways are absent in man and L17@P0: their inhibition is expected to affect the metabolism of L18@P0: Mycobacterium tuberculosis at multiple sites. Our L19@P0: data demonstrate that the pathogen synthesizes pyridoxal 5-phosphate (PLP), the bioactive form of L20@P0: vitamin B6, by a heteromeric PLP synthase composed L21@P0: of Pdx1 (Rv2606c) and Pdx2 (Rv2604c). Disruption of L22@P0: the pdx1 gene generated a strictly B6 auxotrophic M. L23@P0: tuberculosis mutant, Dpdx1. Removal of the cofactor L24@P0: during exponential growth or stationary phase demonstrated the essentiality of vitamin B6 biosynthesis L25@P0: for growth and survival of the pathogen in culture. In L26@P0: a tuberculosis dormancy model based on gradual L27@P0: oxygen depletion, de novo biosynthesis of PLP was L28@P0: required for regrowth of the bacillus after direct L29@P0: oxygen exposure. The Dpdx1 mutant showed a severe L30@P0: growth defect in immunocompetent mice: bacilli L31@P0: applied intranasally failed to persist in host tissues L32@P0: and were quickly cleared. We conclude that vitamin L33@P0: B6 biosynthesis is required for survival of M. tuberculosis in vivo and thus might represent a candidate L34@P0: pathway for the development of new antitubercular L35@P0: agents. L36@P0: Introduction L37@P0: Mycobacterium tuberculosis claims almost two million L38@P0: lives annually and emerging drug resistance made the L39@P0: situation more critical during the past decades (Espinal, L40@P0: 2003; Harries and Dye, 2006). To combat tuberculosis L41@P0: attractive drug targets are required to discover new and L42@P0: effective antibiotics. Pathways present in the pathogen L43@P0: but absent in the host are of particular interest. A whole L44@P0: genome analysis predicted the capability of M. tuberculosis to synthesize vitamin B6, one of the essential components of the human diet (Cole et al., 1998). The term L45@P0: ‘vitamin B6’ refers to the vitamers pyridoxine, pyridoxal, L46@P0: pyridoxamine and their respective 5-phosphoesters. Two L47@P0: independent pathways to generate pyridoxal 5-phosphate L48@P0: (PLP), the bioactive form of vitamin B6 are known. They L49@P0: were distinguished by involvement of the metabolite L50@P0: deoxyxylose 5-phosphate (DXP) and named accordingly L51@P0: (Fitzpatrick et al., 2007). The ‘DXP-dependent’ pathway L52@P0: limited to a small number of bacteria consists of seven L53@P0: enzymatic steps and was extensively studied in Escherichia coli (Lam and Winkler, 1990; 1992; Zhao and L54@P0: Winkler, 1994; 1995; 1996; Zhao et al., 1995; Hill et al., L55@P0: 1996). The increasing availability of genomic data made L56@P0: clear that the ‘DXP-independent’ route is wide-spread L57@P0: among archaea, plants, fungi and most bacteria including L58@P0: the tubercle bacillus (Mittenhuber, 2001). Remarkably, L59@P0: about 4% of all classified enzymes depend on PLP as L60@P0: cofactor, highlighting the enormous functional diversity of L61@P0: the vitamin (Mozzarelli and Bettati, 2006; Fitzpatrick et al., L62@P0: 2007). M. tuberculosis possesses 58 genes encoding proteins that carry a PLP binding motif (Cole et al., 1998; L63@P0: Percudani and Peracchi, 2009). Out of those genes 21 L64@P0: were identified as essential for growth in vitro and most of L65@P0: them are functionally related to the amino acid metabolism (Sassetti et al., 2003). Further implications of PLP in L66@P0: mycobacteria include the biosynthesis of vitamins B7 L67@P0: (biotin), B9 (folate) and B12 (cobalamin), the formation of L68@P0: cell wall components and building blocks of DNA (Cole L69@P0: et al., 1998; Strych et al., 2001; Percudani and Peracchi, L70@P0: 2009). In addition, vitamin B6 was reported to be a potent L71@P0: quencher of reactive oxygen intermediates (Ehrenshaft L72@P0: et al., 1999; Jain and Lim, 2001; Matxain et al., 2009). By converting glutamine into L87@P1: glutamate, Pdx2 generates ammonia, which is used by L88@P1: Pdx1 to synthesize PLP from a 5 and a 3 carbon sugar L89@P1: (Fig. 1A). To date the PLP synthase of many organisms L90@P1: including Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Arabidopsis L91@P1: thaliana, Bacillus subtilis and the malarial parasite Plasmodium falciparum have been characterized (Dong et al., L92@P1: 2004; Raschle et al., 2005; Tambasco-Studart et al., L93@P1: 2005; Wrenger et al., 2005; Gengenbacher et al., 2006). L94@P1: The respective genes pdx1 (Rv2606c) and 2 (Rv2604c) L95@P1: were annotated in the M. tuberculosis genome and their L96@P1: epidemiological conservation was demonstrated by the L97@P1: analysis of 100 clinical isolates from tuberculosis patients L98@P1: (Cole et al., 1998; Tsolaki et al., 2004). The fact that M. L99@P1: leprae, thought to contain the minimal gene set of a virulent mycobacterium, also possesses pdx1 and 2 points to L100@P1: the importance of these genes for pathogenesis (Cole L101@P1: et al., 2001). Neither of the two genes was identified as L102@P1: essential for growth of M. tuberculosis in vitro (due to the L103@P1: presence of exogenous vitamin B6) or in vivo using the L104@P1: whole genome screening approach TraSH (Sassetti and L105@P1: Rubin, 2003; Sassetti et al., 2003). Although, those L106@P1: genetic studies are of great value they are not expected L107@P1: to be definitive. Whether the tubercle bacillus requires L108@P1: de novo PLP biosynthesis for survival and virulence L109@P1: remained unclear and is topic of the current investigation. L141@P2: A pdx1 loss-of-function mutant of M. tuberculosis is fully L142@P2: auxotrophic for vitamin B6 L143@P2: To address the function of PLP biosynthesis in M. tuberculosis,a pdx1 knockout mutant (Dpdx1) was generated L144@P2: via homologous recombination and confirmed by Southern blotting (Fig. S1). As a control, the knockout strain L145@P2: was genetically complemented with a wild-type copy of L146@P2: pdx1 (Dpdx1comp) under the control of its native promoter. The Dpdx1 mutant was not able to multiply in L147@P2: vitamin B6-deficient medium, whereas wild-type M. L148@P2: tuberculosis and the complemented strain showed L149@P2: typical growth curves (Fig. 2A). This demonstrates that L150@P2: PLP is essential for growth in vitro. We then analysed the L151@P2: growth of Dpdx1 in the presence of varying concentrations of exogenous pyridoxine, a stable B6 vitamer, to L152@P2: determine the pathogen’s uptake capability and physiological requirement for the vitamin. The chemical L153@P2: complementation of the Dpdx1 strain with pyridoxine L154@P2: was concentration dependent and optimal growth was L155@P2: restored at 5 mM (Fig. 2A). Lower concentrations of pyridoxine up to 0.5 mM impaired replication, whereas 50 mM L156@P2: proved to be slightly toxic. L186@P3: tuberculosis is essential for direct regrowth on agar L187@P3: Current working models suggest that the prolonged chemotherapy required to cure tuberculosis is due to a L188@P3: defined subpopulation of hypoxic non-replicating bacilli. L189@P3: The obligate aerobic pathogen requires oxygen for growth L190@P3: but not for survival (Barry et al., 2009). Larry Wayne first L191@P3: introduced a culture model based on gradual oxygen L192@P3: deprivation to study non-replicating persistence of the L193@P3: tubercle bacillus (Wayne and Hayes, 1996; Wayne and L194@P3: Sohaskey, 2001). A Western blot analysis revealed that L195@P3: wild-type M. tuberculosis upregulated the PLP synthase in L196@P3: the Wayne model of dormancy (Fig. 3A). Compared with L197@P3: the wild-type or the complemented strain, the Dpdx1 L198@P3: mutant showed a significant loss of viability in nonreplicating Wayne cultures (Fig. 3B, triangles, broken line) L199@P3: when samples were directly plated on agar. However, L200@P3: when the respective Dpdx1 samples were re-aerated in L201@P3: liquid medium prior to plating, the colony-forming units L202@P3: (cfu) were comparable to the controls (Fig. 3B, triangles, L203@P3: straight line). This suggests that disruption of the pdx1 L204@P3: gene did not kill the hypoxic non-replicating bacillus, but L205@P3: made it sensitive to sudden and direct oxygen exposure L206@P3: and thereby prevented regrowth. To address the question, L207@P3: why the ‘re-aeration phenotype’ of Dpdx1 bacilli was not L208@P3: compensated by exogenous vitamin B6 present in all L209@P3: culture media, we analysed the pathogen’s uptake of L210@P3: radiolabelled pyridoxine under aerobic and hypoxic conditions (Fig. 3C). Both wild-type organisms and the Dpdx1 L211@P3: mutant did incorporate pyridoxine during the initial growth L212@P3: phase in the anaerobic shift culture model, while oxygen L213@P3: was present. However, no further uptake of pyridoxine L214@P3: occurred once the two strains entered the oxygen-starved L215@P3: non-replicating state. L237@P3: Vitamin B6 biosynthesis of the tubercle bacillus 983 L238@P3-4: © 2010 Blackwell Publishing Ltd, Molecular Microbiology, 78, 980–988M. tuberculosis requires the PLP biosynthesis for L239@P4: survival in vivo L240@P4: To study the role of pdx1 in virulence, we infected immunocompetent mice with the Dpdx1 mutant and monitored L241@P4: bacterial numbers in lungs and spleen over time. The L242@P4: pdx1 loss-of-function strain was severely attenuated in L243@P4: vivo: at 7 days post infection, the burden of viable Dpdx1 L244@P4: bacilli in lungs was about 1.0 log lower than that of the L245@P4: wild-type control (Fig. 4A). On day 28 the difference was L246@P4: more than 5.0 logs and the number of Dpdx1 organisms L247@P4: dropped below the limit of detection. From day 42 L248@P4: onwards until the end of the experiment on day 84 neither L249@P4: Dpdx1 bacilli nor any revertants were observed. Additionally, the Dpdx1 mutant did not cause any visible gross L250@P4: pulmonary pathology nor was it capable of infecting the L251@P4: spleen (Fig. 4A and B). Genetic complementation L252@P4: restored virulence, demonstrating that the severe growth L253@P4: defect of Dpdx1 in mice was solely due to the disruption of L254@P4: the pdx1 gene. Our data show that bacterial de novo L255@P4: vitamin B6 biosynthesis is essential for survival and virulence of M. tuberculosis in the mouse model. L256@P4: Discussion L257@P4: We have demonstrated that M. tuberculosis synthesizes L258@P4: PLP via the ‘DXP-independent’ pathway by employing a L259@P4: synthase composed of Pdx1 and Pdx2 in line with L260@P4: reports from other species (Fig. 1) (Dong et al., 2004; L261@P4: Raschle et al., 2005; Tambasco-Studart et al., 2005; L262@P4: Gengenbacher et al., 2006; Knockel et al., 2007). Disruption of the pdx1 gene made the pathogen auxotrophic for L263@P4: vitamin B6. Furthermore, we could fully complement the L264@P4: phenotype in vitro by pdx1 under the control of its native L265@P4: promoter (Fig. 2A). This suggests that the downstream L266@P4: genes tesB2 and pdx2 in the knockout and complemented strain were expressed by the hygromycin promoter and thereby allowed formation of the PLP L267@P4: synthase by Pdx1 and Pdx2. L268@P4: Removal of exogenous vitamin B6 during exponential L269@P4: growth and aerated stationary phase resulted in the death L270@P4: of the bacillus, proving the essentiality of the PLP synthase in vitro (Fig. 2B and C). Hypoxic non-replicating L271@P4: cultures of wild-type M. tuberculosis overexpressed the L272@P4: PLP synthase. Surprisingly, Dpdx1 bacilli were impaired L273@P4: for regrowth upon oxygen exposure by direct plating on L274@P4: agar, but the loss of viability was prevented by re-aeration L275@P4: in liquid medium before cfu determination (Fig. 3B). Previous reports provided evidence that vitamin B6 can act L276@P4: as potent quencher of reactive oxygen species (Ehrenshaft et al., 1999; Jain and Lim, 2001; Matxain et al., L277@P4: 2009). Directly plated hypoxic non-replicating Dpdx1 L278@P4: bacilli probably have lost viability because of a lack of L279@P4: protection from oxygen radicals by vitamin B6. However, L280@P4: under aerated conditions wild-type organisms and the L281@P4: Dpdx1 mutant showed similar susceptibility to oxidative L282@P4: stress inducing agents (Fig. S2). An increased demand of L283@P4: PLP during dormancy is unlikely, as the major functions of L284@P4: vitamin B6 are related to amino acid metabolism and L285@P4: therefore to growth (Cole et al., 1998; Sassetti et al., L286@P4: 2003; Percudani and Peracchi, 2009). As a L306@P5: result of the multiple metabolic functions of vitamin B6 our L307@P5: results obtained from the Wayne model remain difficult L308@P5: to interpret and further experiments are required for L309@P5: clarification. L310@P5: Mycobacterium tuberculosis resides inside macrophages and extracellularly. Whether the intracellular bacillus L311@P5: can access host derived vitamin B6 and therefore would L312@P5: be resistant to inhibition of its PLP synthase is unclear. L313@P5: When we analysed the Dpdx1 mutant in a macrophage L314@P5: culture model, we did not observe any significant defect in L315@P5: survival compared with the wild-type or the complemented strain (Fig. S3). However, media required to maintain macrophages contained 4.9 mM pyridoxine, enough L316@P5: to allow optimal growth of M. tuberculosis in aerated cultures (Fig. 2A). Thus, the result might not reflect the L317@P5: situation in vivo. To gain further insights, we infected L318@P5: immunocompetent mice with the Dpdx1 mutant and L319@P5: observed a severe growth and survival defect, suggesting L320@P5: that vitamin B6 availability in the host is insufficient to L321@P5: support the pathogen in vivo (Fig. 4A). We did not observe L322@P5: secondary infection of the spleen, probably because of L323@P5: the clearance of Dpdx1 bacilli from the lungs, the primary L324@P5: site of infection (Fig. 4B). L325@P5: The most accurate estimation for overall vitamin B6 in L326@P5: the human body is the blood plasma concentration of PLP L327@P5: (Lui et al., 1985). Depending on nutritional and epidemiological influences, the presence of PLP in blood plasma of L328@P5: man fluctuates between 20 and 120 nM (Morris et al., L329@P5: 2008) or between 100 and 200 nM in mice (van de Kamp L330@P5: et al., 1995). However, the phosphorylated PLP molecule L331@P5: is expected to have a low permeability through biological L332@P5: membranes and thus cannot serve as vitamin B6 source L333@P5: for the Dpdx1 mutant in vitro (Fig. S4). The mouse blood L334@P5: plasma concentration of unphosphorylated and therefore L335@P5: membrane permeable B6 vitamers was reported to be L336@P5: < 800 nM. This concentration was insufficient to support L337@P5: optimal growth of the pathogen in vitro (Fig. 2A) (van de L338@P5: Kamp et al., 1995). The fact that we could not recover any L339@P5: bacilli from Dpdx1-infected mice beyond day 42 highlights L340@P5: the extraordinary sensitivity of the pathogen to vitamin B6 L341@P5: shortage. L342@P5: The Dpdx1 mutant has features essential for a successful vaccine candidate: it is attenuated by a non-reverting L343@P5: mutation and is avirulent, comparable to a strain deficient L344@P5: for the biosynthesis of vitamin B5 (Sambandamurthy L345@P5: et al., 2002). Our data warrant further investigation L346@P5: whether a pdx1 knockout could be exploited for vaccine L347@P5: development. In conclusion, the current study reveals the L348@P5: fundamental importance of vitamin B6 biosynthesis for L349@P5: survival and virulence of the tubercle bacillus and thus L350@P5: might offer an interesting pathway for the discovery of L351@P5: new antimycobacterials.
